causes.text: In September 2024, Summit Therapeutics and its partner Akeso reported that their bispecific antibody ivonescimab produced significantly better survival rates than Keytruda in a late-stage trial in China.

source_info.title: Ivonescimab outperforms Keytruda in Chinese trial

effects.text: On November 14 2024, Merck licensed LaNova Medicines' early-stage bispecific antibody LM-299, which targets PD-1 and VEGF, in a deal worth up to $3.3 billion. Merck paid $588 million upfront and agreed to milestone payments of up to $2.7 billion to gain development and commercialization rights to the therapy, bolstering its oncology pipeline.

source_info.title: Merck signs up to $3.3 billion cancer drug deal with LaNova

causal_reasoning_chain.description: Summit Therapeutics and Akeso's announcement that ivonescimab significantly outperformed Keytruda in a Chinese trial alerted industry observers to the disruptive potential of bispecific antibodies targeting PD-1 and VEGF. The news suggested that Keytruda's dominance could be challenged sooner than expected.

Analysts cautioned that if bispecific antibodies gained traction, they could erode Keytruda's multibillion-dollar revenue stream. To hedge against this threat, Merck assessed external candidates that could complement its pipeline and mitigate competitive risks.

On November 14 2024, Merck announced a licensing agreement with LaNova for LM-299, agreeing to pay $588 million upfront and up to $2.7 billion in milestones. By securing its own bispecific antibody targeting PD-1 and VEGF, Merck signalled to investors that it planned to defend its oncology franchise; the early-stage status of the asset led to a muted market response; on 2024-11-14 shares were up about 0.01% versus the prior trading day.

rationale: Evidence that a rival bispecific antibody could outperform Keytruda posed a direct threat to Merck's flagship immunotherapy.  To protect its oncology leadership and prepare for the emergence of dual-target therapies, Merck entered a costly licensing deal to secure access to a similar modality.
counterfactual_analysis: Absent the impressive ivonescimab trial results, Merck may have delayed or foregone licensing a bispecific antibody.  Without a clear competitive threat to Keytruda, the company could have prioritised other therapeutic areas or invested internally rather than paying nearly $3.3 billion for an early-stage asset.

adversarial_confounders.text: BioNTech's acquisition of Biotheus for a PD-1/VEGF bispecific antibody during the same period also signaled rising interest in this class.
adversarial_confounders.impact: Other companies' strategic moves may have influenced Merck's decision alongside the ivonescimab data.

details.commentary: Keytruda's dominance made Merck vulnerable to any rival therapy that could match or beat its survival benefits, especially in large cancer indications. The strong data from ivonescimab raised the threat of a powerful substitute, prompting Merck to license LaNova's bispecific antibody so it could compete rather than cede the next wave of innovation.

details.pestel_factor: Technological - Emergence of bispecific antibody platforms
details.commentary: Rapid advances in bispecific antibody engineering are changing what oncologists and regulators expect from new cancer drugs. Those technological shifts made it strategically sensible for Merck to commit billions of dollars to LM-299 at an early stage, aiming to keep its oncology portfolio aligned with the latest scientific standards.

Each time a competitor releases superior efficacy data, it forces incumbents to invest more in R and D, which then raises the performance bar for the entire field. Merck's licensing move both responds to and reinforces this innovation race, creating a feedback loop in which portfolio gaps are quickly filled by new deals and collaborations.
